analysis.one_liner: Lets struggling borrowers wipe out private student loans in bankruptcy, like other debts.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote in the Senate before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current bankruptcy law, almost no student loan can be wiped out, even private loans from banks, unless the borrower can prove 'undue hardship' in a separate lawsuit-like proceeding. This bill would change that for private education loans: only loans and benefits from the government would remain protected from discharge. Borrowers crushed by private loan debt could treat it like credit card or medical debt in bankruptcy.
analysis.who_benefits: People who took out private student loans from banks and lenders and later fell on hard times, who today must prove 'undue hardship' at a very high bar to escape the debt. The bill narrows the exception so only government-backed loans and benefits stay nondischargeable; private loans could be discharged like other unsecured debts [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the bankruptcy-code provision making private and nonprofit-funded education loans nondischargeable, leaving only government loans, guarantees, and educational benefits protected [S2][S3].
Amends the existing 'undue hardship' exception structure so a debtor can discharge qualified education loans that are not made, insured, or guaranteed by a governmental unit [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private student lenders and banks, which lose the guarantee that their loans follow borrowers for life; they would bear more default losses, which could translate into somewhat higher rates on private student loans.

drawbacks.text: Lenders argue that without lifetime protection, private student loans carry more default risk, so interest rates could rise and some credit to students could dry up.
Federal taxpayer-backed loans would remain protected from discharge, so the bill addresses only the private-loan slice of student debt; borrowers with government loans would see no change [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For borrowers the upside is direct and large: private loans become dischargeable, restoring a basic bankruptcy right that existed until 2005. The cost falls on lenders as higher expected losses, and possibly slightly pricier private loans for future students. Because government loans stay protected, the taxpayer exposure is unchanged. The trade is modest for the industry and significant for the hardest-hit borrowers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and sat there until the Congress ended; the committee never acted on it and the Senate never voted [S5][S1].

narrative.text: Durbin, Franken, and Whitehouse introduced the bill on April 15, 2010 [S3][S4].
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, with no further action recorded for the rest of the 111th Congress [S5].
The Congress ended January 3, 2011 without a committee markup, committee vote, or Senate floor vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private student lenders and banks keep the current law that makes their loans nearly impossible to erase in bankruptcy; borrowers receive no relief.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks [S1][S5].

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on April 15, 2010 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress [S5].

against.name: Private student loan industry
against.role: Lenders holding nondischargeable private education loans
against.what_they_did: Has publicly and repeatedly opposed restoring bankruptcy discharge for private student loans in similar legislative efforts.

sides.party_line_note: Only three Democrats sponsored or cosponsored the bill and no chamber ever voted on it, so no partisan split can be measured from a roll call.

industries.note: The bill repeals the part of bankruptcy law that shields private education loans from discharge [S2][S3]. Lenders' core advantage in this market is that borrowers cannot walk away, so the bill's benefit to struggling borrowers comes directly at the lenders' expense.
The bill keeps government loans, guarantees, and educational benefits nondischargeable [S2][S3]. Taxpayers keep the same protection they have today, so no new federal exposure is created.
